items.title: Why Bigger Context Windows Won't Save Your Agent — Elizabeth Fuentes Leone, AWS
items.description:
A bigger context window won't save your agent. Past a point, it forgets the middle.

Elizabeth Fuentes Leone, developer advocate at AWS, explains why agents break when tools return huge amounts of data, and why bigger context windows aren't the fix: models remember the start and end of a long context but lose the middle. Using the open-source, model-agnostic Strands Agents framework, she walks through four strategies (externalize, select, compress, isolate) with code. She covers sliding-window and summarizing conversation managers, short-term, long-term and graph memory, memory pointers that keep big tool outputs out of context, sharing pointers across a swarm of agents, capping tool calls to stop endless loops, and async handles for slow MCP tools. She ends with the anti-patterns to avoid.

In this talk:
• Why bigger context windows don't fix agents, and how models lose the middle
• Four strategies: externalize, select, compress and isolate
• Memory pointers, conversation managers and multi-agent state in Strands
• Stopping endless tool loops and handling slow MCP tools

items.title: AI Hackers Are Faster Than Your Pen Test — Eli Cohen, Snyk
items.description:
Attackers use AI too, and the fastest AI attack he cites took four minutes. A pen test once or twice a year can't keep up.

Eli Cohen of Snyk, co-founder of the runtime security company Helios, explains why security has to go on the offense in an agent-first world. Developers now ship far more code, much of it insecure, while attackers use frontier models to chain small vulnerabilities into critical ones in minutes. He walks through why traditional tools fall short: static scanning misses runtime issues, dynamic testing misses business logic, and human pen tests are expensive and happen only a few times a year. Then he describes continuous offensive security: AI pen testing on every code change, agent red teaming, and a team of agents (orchestrator, recon, vulnerability hunters, an exploit-validating judge, remediation and reporting), fed with context from other scanners. He ends with four questions to ask any AI pen testing vendor.

In this talk:
• Why AI-generated code and AI-powered attackers break the old security model
• SAST vs DAST vs pen testing, and what each one misses
• How a team of agents runs pen tests and proves exploits on every PR
• Four questions to ask any AI pen testing vendor

items.title: The Software Factory: From Bug Report to Production Code — Davis Palmie, Factory
items.description:
Engineers are going from typing code to governing agents. The next step is a system that turns bug reports into production code.

Davis Palmie, member of technical staff at Factory, explains the software factory: a system of agents that takes input signals like bug reports and user feedback and turns them into production code. He covers the questions every leader asks, from runaway costs and model choice to what happens to engineers and org charts, and argues coding was never the bottleneck: review, debugging, docs and testing are. He lays out the principles a factory needs (model-agnostic, sovereign deployment, integrated across the SDLC, available on every surface), why to start with something narrow like incident triage, and Factory's eight pillars of agent readiness. He closes with why token leaderboards are Goodhart's law in action, and the outcome metrics to track instead.

In this talk:
• What a software factory is, and why coding was never the bottleneck
• Model-agnostic, sovereign and SDLC-wide: principles for a factory
• Agent readiness: eight pillars that help agents and engineers alike
• Metrics that matter: signal-to-production time, interventions, cost per PR

items.title: Why Your AI Agents Can't Talk to Each Other (Yet) — Vlad Luzin, BAND
items.description:
If you run Claude and Codex side by side, you're the router passing messages between them. It doesn't have to be that way.

Vlad Luzin, co-founder and CTO of BAND, argues the future belongs to AI agents talking to other AI agents, inside companies, between companies, and between businesses and consumers. Most of us already run multi-agent systems by hand, copying output between a planning session and a reviewing session, and loop engineering just hands that job to a script. He explains why: a single agent suffers from confirmation bias and attention dilution, no matter how big its context. Then he explains why messaging apps and protocols like MCP and A2A don't solve it, and why connecting agents is a distributed systems problem: ordered real-time transport, persistence, runtime binding, identity and observability. He finishes by launching BAND's interaction layer, with demos of agents onboarding in seconds and Claude Code and Codex working together across users.

In this talk:
• Adversarial agents, loop engineering, and the single-agent bottleneck
• Why Slack, Telegram, MCP and A2A fall short for agent-to-agent work
• What connecting agents really takes: transport, persistence, runtime binding
• Demo: Claude Code, Codex and LangGraph agents collaborating across users

items.title: Why AI Agents Should Have Their Own Sandbox — Philipp Schmid, Google DeepMind
items.description:
Your agent shouldn't run on your laptop. Give it its own computer in the cloud, with one API call.

Philipp Schmid from Google DeepMind walks through the Gemini Interactions API, Google's new API for both models and agents. It handles server-side state, long-running background jobs, and built-in plus custom tools across text, audio and images, and it replaces user/model turns with a timeline of steps. Then he shows the Antigravity agent in the Gemini API, which runs the same harness as Antigravity in its own managed cloud sandbox. Agents can run code, install tools, share environments with other agents and pick up skills and AGENTS.md files automatically. He covers the Agents API for packaging reusable agents, the new Gemini API CLI, and demos an AI talk radio show generated from one prompt.

In this talk:
• The Interactions API: one interface for models and agents
• Why steps replace user/model turns for agentic apps
• Managed sandboxes: persistent, shareable environments with skills built in
• Demo: an AI talk radio agent built from an AGENTS.md file and skills

items.title: Building resilient systems with Sam Newman
items.description:
Sam Newman wrote one of the most-read books about microservices (“Building Microservices”), but he calls them an architecture of “last resort.”

In this episode of the Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Sam explains his thinking on this, and he’s certainly well placed to do so; he was in the room when the term “microservices” was coined. We discuss what teams get wrong when adopting microservices, why independent deployment matters, and how microservices can help teams work more autonomously.

We also delve into his new book, ‘Building Resilient Distributed Systems’, and Sam explains his three rules for distributed systems, why observability is essential, and also why it’s vital to take business context into account when deciding whether to fail open or fail closed on errors.

We also explore how AI is changing software development, from specs versus code as a source of truth to cognitive debt and cognitive surrender. Sam shares how modular architecture can help teams experiment with AI while maintaining understanding of the systems being built.

items.title: Redesigning How Software Gets Built With AI Agents — Sonar & McKinsey Panel
items.description:
Most companies say they've deployed AI agents. Fewer than a third say it's paying off. What do the rest do differently?

A panel with Sonar CEO Tariq Shaukat and Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, former CEO of Gitar (now part of Sonar) and former head of Uber's developer platform, moderated by McKinsey. Research with Sonar found the teams getting real results from agents change three things: their process, their tooling and, most often overlooked, their people and roles. Tariq explains why lighthouse teams alone don't spread new habits, and why engineers need to make implicit knowledge explicit and get great at critical thinking, because AI always sounds sure. Ali covers how big companies can borrow from small teams through their platform orgs, and walks through how trust builds step by step: from AI reviews, to blocking on issues, to autofix, to auto-approve and auto-merge.

In this talk:
• Three factors behind teams that scale agents: process, tooling and people
• Why role models and lighthouse teams aren't enough on their own
• The skills that matter now: explicit thinking, critical thinking, generalists
• How trust grows from AI code review to fully automated merges

items.title: From 36% to 100%: How Self-Improving Agents Write Their Own Skills — Rafal Wilinski, Runlayer
items.description:
When one agent finally cracks a hard problem, what if every agent in the company learned it too?

Rafal Wilinski, founding engineer at Runlayer, shows how to go from one self-improving agent to a self-improving company. He explains why skills matter more as agents work longer (a bad start can send them down an hours-long rabbit hole) and the three problems holding skills back: they're built for developers, nobody has time to write them, and many clients don't support them. His fix is to deliver skills over MCP from one governed server, then let agents write their own skills by distilling successful and failed runs, an idea borrowed from the Voyager Minecraft paper. In one test, a distilled skill took a task from 36% success to 100%. Multiply that across every agent and you get an organizational flywheel that keeps your hard-won knowledge even as models change.

In this talk:
• What skills are, and why they matter more as agents run longer
• Using MCP as the distribution layer for skills across the whole company
• Distilling skills from agent traces, and why failed runs teach the most
• The organizational flywheel: knowledge competitors can't copy

Grep or Embeddings? Agentic Search Over Company Documents — George He, LlamaIndex
items.description:
Grep works great on a codebase. Try it on millions of PDFs, slides and scanned schematics.

George He, head of engineering at LlamaIndex, explains when agents need pre-indexed search and when plain file traversal is enough. Claude Code skipped embeddings because code is small, text-based, local and full of breadcrumbs. Company data is huge, messy, multimodal and permissioned. He shows how to give an agent a harness of tools so it can choose: hybrid retrieval as a compass, then listing, metadata filtering, grep and reading to dig in, plus parsed text and page screenshots for complex documents. He covers parsing with LlamaParse and the open-source LiteParse, permissions and freshness in production, and the ingest-parse-index pipeline. Then he demos an agent building a cash-flow table from 135 Alphabet financial filings, grounded in the source files.

In this talk:
• Why Claude Code's grep approach works for code but breaks on company documents
• Hybrid search as a compass, then grep and read to ground the answer
• Parsing complex PDFs, tables and schematics, with page screenshots
• Production concerns: multi-tenancy, permissions and data freshness

items.title: Every AI Company Is Accidentally Building a Bank — Dor Sasson, Stigg
items.description:
In one month, three of the biggest AI companies had a pricing emergency. Dor Sasson says it was really an infrastructure problem.

Dor Sasson, co-founder and CEO of Stigg, argues that every AI company is accidentally building a bank. He starts with the April pricing scramble, when Anthropic cut third-party agents like OpenClaw off its subscription plans, OpenAI changed its Pro tier, and GitHub pulled free Copilot access, plus stories of companies burning through their AI budgets in weeks. The common problem: usage gets checked after the invoice, not before. He makes the case for checking entitlements synchronously before inference and settling asynchronously after, like an ATM, and points to OpenAI's own published architecture. He covers the banking ideas AI products now need, from hold-and-settle and double-entry bookkeeping to credit sources and spend caps across teams, users and agents.

In this talk:
• Why AI pricing emergencies are really infrastructure problems
• Check before you spend: synchronous checks, asynchronous settlement
• Concurrency, double spend, and drawing down from different credit pools
• Four patterns for selling AI at scale, from reserve-and-settle to spend visibility

items.title: The 6 Pillars of an Agentic Harness for Production — Varun Krovvidi, Resolve AI
items.description:
AI changed how we write code. But 70% of engineering time goes to running and fixing it.

Varun Krovvidi, product marketing lead at Resolve AI, explains why AI that writes code well still struggles to run production. Code is self-documenting, modular and a single domain. Production spans code, infrastructure, telemetry and many teams, and needs one correct answer. He covers where agents crack as you scale: anchoring bias and the model treadmill, too much or too little context, coherent answers that aren't causal, missing guardrails, and no learning across investigations. Then he lays out six pillars of a harness that fixes them: model orchestration, context engineering, causal reasoning, governed actions, learning systems and evals. He finishes with a demo of Resolve AI turning a Grafana alert into a root cause, ruling out a coincidental GCP outage, and holding its ground when pushed.

In this talk:
• Why coding is easy for AI and production isn't
• Five ways production agents break as they scale
• Six pillars: orchestration, context, causal reasoning, governed actions, learning, evals
• Demo: from Slack alert to root cause with ruled-out theories

items.title: Toppling Saddam was the easy part - Sarah Paine
Is Speculative Decoding Worth It? Profiling vLLM on NVIDIA Blackwell — Akamai
items.description:
A small model guesses the next few tokens. The big model checks them in one pass. When is that worth it?

Sheilah Kirui, developer advocate at Akamai, explains speculative decoding and how to tell whether it's worth turning on. She walks through the prefill and decode phases of inference, how a small draft model proposes tokens that the target model verifies in a single forward pass, and the memory cost of hosting a second model and its KV cache. She covers how to choose a draft model, then demos both setups side by side with vLLM on a single NVIDIA Blackwell GPU: structured output ran 1.6x faster with a high acceptance rate, while creative writing saw far lower acceptance. She also explains why long-context and high-concurrency workloads gain less.

In this talk:
• Prefill vs decode, and what speculative decoding speeds up
• Choosing a draft model: size, shared tokenizer, cost and accuracy
• Demo: acceptance rate on structured vs creative tasks in vLLM
• When it's worth it: spare VRAM, small batches, structured output, short context

items.title: Move Fast and Don't Break Things: Scaling Databases for the AI Era — PlanetScale
items.description:
AI agents are multiplying traffic overnight. Here's how to ship fast without taking your database down with it.

Ben Dicken from PlanetScale argues you no longer have to choose between moving fast and keeping things up. He covers the principles behind reliable infrastructure, isolation and redundancy, then how to scale with sharding, back pressure and decoupling, the same ideas PlanetScale uses to run databases for fast-growing AI companies like Cursor. Then he gets to agents: how a simple VSchema JSON file lets an agent design a sharding plan for Vitess, how Traffic Control sets resource budgets so a surge of agent traffic degrades gracefully instead of crashing, and how database branching, deploy requests and one-click reverts let agents change schemas safely. His point: good developer experience turns out to be good primitives for AI.

In this talk:
• Isolation and redundancy, and why failures become weekly at scale
• Sharding, back pressure and decoupling explained
• Letting agents design a Vitess sharding scheme from a JSON VSchema
• Traffic Control budgets, schema branching and one-click reverts for agents

items.title: Why Building an Eval Platform Is Harder Than It Looks — Braintrust
items.description:
Most teams start their evals in a spreadsheet. Here's what happens when they try to grow out of it.

Hossein Niazmandi, who leads solutions engineering in the West at Braintrust, explains why measuring agent quality is much more than putting a UI on a spreadsheet. He covers the two pillars of agent quality, evals before production and observability after, and why non-deterministic LLMs make both necessary. Then he walks through the stages teams go through: spreadsheets, a custom UI, side-by-side experiments for PMs and domain experts, and finally a flywheel that turns production failures into test cases. At that point the hard part becomes the data: traces that are huge, nested JSON, needing both real-time and long-running queries, which is why Braintrust built BTQL. He closes with agents running evals themselves and surfacing failures nobody thought to look for.

In this talk:
• Evals vs observability, and why you need both
• The stages of eval maturity, from spreadsheets to a production flywheel
• Why agent traces break typical data warehouses
• Letting coding agents run evals while humans review the results

items.title: The Self-Improving OSS Agent Stack — Marc Klingen, Langfuse
items.description:
Improving an agent used to mean a human reading traces every week. Now agents can do most of that loop for you.

Marc Klingen, co-founder of Langfuse, shows how teams are moving from manually improving their agents to letting AI run the improvement loop. He explains the reference stack that emerged for building agents, which connects online tracing and monitoring with offline datasets, experiments and evals, and maps the layers of loops from next-token prediction up to human goal-setting. AI is already good at proposing fixes, and teams are starting to use it to maintain datasets and eval criteria too, while humans stay in charge of direction. In a demo, a coding agent uses Langfuse's agent skills to find that Langfuse's own changelog writer leaks internal jargon, updates the evals, and back-tests a better version before shipping it.

In this talk:
• The online + offline loop: traces, datasets, experiments and evals
• Where humans still need to stay in the loop, and where AI can take over
• Using implicit user signals like edits and approvals as feedback
• Why owning your trace data matters when agents read far more of it

items.title: Harness Engineering: How to Build a Software Factory — Dru Knox, Tessl
items.description:
In a software factory, agents write everything your users get. Your engineers build the factory.

Dru Knox, head of product and design at Tessl, explains harness engineering (some now call it loop engineering), the discipline that takes a team from using coding agents to running a software factory. He defines a factory by three metrics: autonomy, automation and quality. He breaks the work into inner, outer and meta loops, and explains why harness engineering is hard: the field changes weekly, the work is unplanned, and the signals you need are stuck in local logs. Then he lays out three layers to build, a control plane, an agent-ready stack and improvement loops, and shows how Tessl's skills registry, Tessl Agent and Tessl Launch help you get there one workflow at a time.

In this talk:
• What a software factory is, and why the real payoff is higher quality, not just speed
• Inner, outer and meta loops, and what each one improves
• The three layers: control plane, agent-ready infrastructure, improvement loops
• Metrics to track: manual takeovers, human PR comments, PRs started without a human

items.title: Schema Registry: The Contract Enforcer You Need  #infoq
items.description:
A Schema Registry isn’t just storage. It’s your event-driven architecture’s contract enforcer.

Configured for compatibility, it blocks breaking schema changes before they ever hit production.

➡️ No broken consumers
➡️ No downstream fire drills
➡️ Just enforced contracts
